subject: Hierarchical model and positive posterior probabilities near the boundaries

messages.author: f0ede2122c290390
messages.subject: Hierarchical model and positive posterior probabilities near the boundaries
parts:
I know it is mentioned in the manual that Stan won't sample well near the boundaries of constrained parameters, but I just wanted to suggest more explicit warnings about this perhaps somewhere in the manual or in Google group FAQ, given the popularity of Bayesian hierarchical models and potentially substantial impact (overestimates of scale parameters) on the inference caused by this "boundary effect."

To help me explain the issue, let me briefly provide the context. I have been hired by a data consulting company to speed up the Bayesian hierarchical model they have been using for a while. I decided to use an approach similar to INLA (except that everything was conjugate in the model, so no approximation errors from Laplace approximation) and analytically integrated out all the latent parameters to get the marginal likelihood for the scale parameters. Then I computed the posterior mean of the latent parameters using a numerical integration and discovered that my estimates and Stan's estimates were similar but quite noticeably different (and I ran Stan for very long time to ensure the convergence).

Here is what I eventually discovered (using simulated data) and I will speak in terms of a simple random effect model as in Gelman 2006 to be concrete. With a uniform (or half-Cauchy) prior on the scale parameter of group effects, there can be substantial posterior probabilities near the boundary (scale = 0). But Stan does not sample very well near the boundary and this leads to an overestimate of the scale of the group effects. Since the scale parameter is overestimated, the resulting estimates of the group effects are less "shrunk" toward the overall mean. 

A Bayesian hierarchical model is a popular way to obtain a shrinkage estimator and I bet many people try to fit such models with Stan, so I think the boundary effect and potential overestimates of scale parameters warrant more explicit warnings. In one of the simulated data I cooked up, the estimates of the latent parameters from Stan had 50% larger MSE than the MSE I obtained using the numerical integration.

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical model and positive posterior probabilities near the boundaries
parts:
There is a Bayesian thing going on here.  If the true value of the parameter is zero, but the prior is not centered at zero (which it can’t be, since the parameter is restricted to be nonnegative), then Bayes will necessarily “shrink” the estimate toward the prior, and you’ll get a positive, nonzero parameter estimate.

What I’m getting at is, I think it’s still not clear whether the problem is with Stan not converging to the posterior, or maybe Stan’s giving the right answer given the model you’re supplying.

A

messages.author: f0ede2122c290390
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical model and positive posterior probabilities near the boundaries
parts:
I am not looking at the posterior mean of the hyper parameters, but the posterior distributions. The model is a type of a Gaussian process regression and I have an analytical expression (up to constant) for the posterior distributions of the three scale parameters, so I can easily and accurately estimate the marginal distributions of the scale parameters via numerical integration. This clearly shows that the mode is at (or very close to) scale = 0, but the samples from Stan are clearly bounded away from zero.

To ensure that my own code is right, I also tried putting an informative prior so that the posterior distribution vanishes at scale = 0, and in this case the numerically approximated posterior distribution and histogram from a long Stan run coincide almost exactly.

I think this phenomenon also makes sense theoretically; as I understand, Stan transformed a bounded interval into an infinite interval when given constraints, right? If there were indeed positive probability density at the boundary, this transformation results in a heavy tailed distribution with substantial mass close to infinity. It may well take impractically long time for HMC or NUTS to the tail of such distributions. Given that the geometric ergodicity of MALA is violated for such a heavy tailed distribution (Roberts and Tweedie 1996), I would not be surprised if HMC and NUTS also are not geometrically ergodic either for a heavy tailed distribution.

parts:
> On Jun 25, 2015, at 6:09 PM, Akihiko Nishimura <akihiko_...@hotmail.com> wrote:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1508#issuecomment-115430800

> To help me explain the issue, let me briefly provide the context. I have been hired by a data consulting company to speed up the Bayesian hierarchical model they have been using for a while. I decided to use an approach similar to INLA (except that everything was conjugate in the model, so no approximation errors from Laplace approximation) and analytically integrated out all the latent parameters to get the marginal likelihood for the scale parameters. Then I computed the posterior mean of the latent parameters using a numerical integration and discovered that my estimates and Stan's estimates were similar but quite noticeably different (and I ran Stan for very long time to ensure the convergence).

You need to run long enough that all the R-hat values from
multiple chains are near 1.

> Here is what I eventually discovered (using simulated data) and I will speak in terms of a simple random effect model as in Gelman 2006 to be concrete. With a uniform (or half-Cauchy) prior on the scale parameter of group effects, there can be substantial posterior probabilities near the boundary (scale = 0). But Stan does not sample very well near the boundary and this leads to an overestimate of the scale of the group effects.

How near the boundary are we talking? Stan does Bayesian inference,
so it's never going to push the posterior mean to zero.
> Since the scale parameter is overestimated, the resulting estimates of the group effects are less "shrunk" toward the overall mean.
How do you know the scale parameter is overestimated?
> A Bayesian hierarchical model is a popular way to obtain a shrinkage estimator and I bet many people try to fit such models with Stan,

:-) We're well aware of this, though we call it "pooling"
rather than "shrinkage" because the posterior mean is not
always zero.

> so I think the boundary effect and potential overestimates of scale parameters warrant more explicit warnings. In one of the simulated data I cooked up, the estimates of the latent parameters from Stan had 50% larger MSE than the MSE I obtained using the numerical integration.

I take it you're talking about using the posterior mean as
an estimate? It's set up to minimize expected square error of
the estimators *relative to the model*. When you add priors, that's
not the same as the MLE, which will literally minimize square error
on the training data for straight-up linear regression.

If you can send us a fake data example and model, we can try to understand
what's going on.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical model and positive posterior probabilities near the boundaries
parts:
On Jun 25, 2015, at 9:41 PM, Akihiko Nishimura <akihiko_...@hotmail.com> wrote:

I am not looking at the posterior mean of the hyper parameters, but the posterior distributions.

But those aren't points.  How do you estimate square error with
a distribution?  In expectation?

The model is a type of a Gaussian process regression and I have an analytical expression (up to constant) for the posterior distributions of the three scale parameters, so I can easily and accurately estimate the marginal distributions of the scale parameters via numerical integration. This clearly shows that the mode is at (or very close to) scale = 0, but the samples from Stan are clearly bounded away from zero.

But Bayesian inference doesn't care about the mode.  But it
will correspond to the mean in a symmetric distribution, but
your posterior for a scale parameter can't be symmetric, because
it's bounded below at 0 and has support on (0, inf).  (Actually,
I'm just guessing here.)

To ensure that my own code is right, I also tried putting an informative prior so that the posterior distribution vanishes at scale = 0, and in this case the numerically approximated posterior distribution and histogram from a long Stan run coincide almost exactly.

I think this phenomenon also makes sense theoretically; as I understand, Stan transformed a bounded interval into an infinite interval when given constraints, right?

Right --- if you supply <lower=0>, we log transform
the parameter for sampling, and apply the appropriate Jacobian
adjustment.  And you only need to get to -700 or so to
underflow to 0 using the inverse transform, exp().
If there were indeed positive probability density at the boundary, this transformation results in a heavy tailed distribution with substantial mass close to infinity.

Not quite.  There's a positive *density* at the boundary, but
that doesn't translate into heavy mass near infinity because things
get very stretched out under the log transform.  

And then there's the Jacobian.

Of course, it depends where you start, because log transforming
an improper uniform on (0, inf) to (-inf, inf) produces an improper
result.

Here's a histogram of the log transformed half Cauchy(0, 2.5),
produced in R with:

hist(log(abs(rt(1000000, 1, 2.5))), breaks=50)

It may well take impractically long time for HMC or NUTS to the tail of such distributions. Given that the geometric ergodicity of MALA is violated for such a heavy tailed distribution (Roberts and Tweedie 1996), I would not be surprised if HMC and NUTS also are not geometrically ergodic either for a heavy tailed distribution.

You're right that if the distribution's heavy tailed enough (as in
a Cauchy) or light tailed enough (in an untransformed triangle distribution,
say), then you can run into problems. 

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical model and positive posterior probabilities near the boundaries
parts:
Sorry I haven't gotten back to you on this. We've been
swamped preparing a course and getting Stan 2.7 out.

The R-hat measure isn't whether the 10 different chains together
explored the space, but rather whether they each explored the space.
So we're measuring within-chain means and variances and comparing to
the result of pooling across chains, under the assumption the answer
should be the same. We use that to compute n_eff as well as R-hat.

Strong correlations can certainly break sampling efficiency. Sometimes
reparameterizing the model with the same posterior but a different
sampling basis can help.

- Bob
